descriptions: The Lord who reveals all scripture through five faces, as five streams (Kāmika pūrva 1.20–27).
Śiva's knowledge (śivajñāna) is the higher knowledge revealing the Lord; lower knowledges reveal the bound soul and its bonds (Kāmika pūrva 1.14–17).
In the Kashmirian reading, the Lord's teaching is one, graded as difference (Śiva tantras), difference-in-identity (Rudra tantras) and non-difference (Bhairava tantras) (Jayaratha on TĀ 1.18).
relation_to_self: Disputed within the Mantramārga: the Siddhānta holds the soul eternally distinct, becoming equal to Śiva in liberation; the Bhairava-tantra exegetes of Kashmir hold identity.
relation_to_world: The Lord acts on the world through his power(s) and mantras; the Siddhānta treats māyā as a real material cause distinct from Śiva, the non-dual exegetes as Śiva's self-manifestation.
caveat: The Mantramārga is not doctrinally uniform. The Saiddhāntikas reject the non-dual reading of their scriptures and the identity of soul and Śiva; a one-truth reading must record this denial.

descriptions: Svacchandabhairava, a form of Aghora/Bhairava, worshipped with his consort Aghoreśvarī.
caveat: Known here only at catalogue level; the Svacchandatantra's own doctrine is recorded by U19.

descriptions: The supreme is Bhairava in union with his power(s); in later Vidyāpīṭha texts the goddess becomes primary.
caveat: Catalogue-level summary; the doctrinal views of the Trika and Kālīkula are recorded by U19/U24.

descriptions: The ṣāḍguṇya — possessor of the six qualities — is the supreme Brahman, cause of all causes, free of all pairs of opposites and all limiting adjuncts (Ahirbudhnya 2.53).
Knowledge is the very form of Brahman; power, lordship, strength, virility and splendour are aspects of that knowledge (Ahirbudhnya 2.56–62).
Śrī/Lakṣmī is his eternal Śakti, inseparable from him, who performs his five acts (Lakṣmī Tantra 12.12–14).
negations: He is called 'without qualities' (nirguṇa) because he is untouched by the qualities of prakṛti (Ahirbudhnya 2.55).
relation_to_self: Individual souls depend on Bhagavān; by his grace (śaktipāta) their karmas are equalised and they are lifted from saṃsāra to his presence.
relation_to_world: The world issues from his Śakti in a pure creation (the vyūhas) and an other-than-pure creation from prakṛti.
caveat: Saṃhitās differ in emphasis (e.g. the Lakṣmī Tantra's Śakti-centred account); Śrīvaiṣṇava readers interpret the Pāñcarātra within qualified non-dualism. The tradition insists on a personal Lord and would reject reading him as an impersonal absolute.

names.name: the five forms: Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Aniruddha

descriptions: Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman, the highest Self; his highest form is subtle, imperishable and partless (niṣkala); his gross form with parts (sakala) is the cause of all (Kriyādhikāra 11.148–150).
relation_to_self: The worshipper attains Viṣṇu's world and nearness to him in graded forms of liberation (sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya).
relation_to_world: Nārāyaṇa is the cause of the whole world; Vikhanas, author of the Sūtra, is born of him (Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa).
caveat: The Vaikhānasas insist on the Vedic identity of their worship and would reject being classed with tantric Āgama theologies.

names.name: the seven installed deities as forms of the supreme

descriptions: From the supreme Lord endowed with existence, consciousness and bliss, and with parts (sakala), arose Śakti; from her Nāda; from Nāda, Bindu (Śāradātilaka 1.7).
caveat: Kerala tantra is a ritual tradition serving several deities; it has no single systematic theology. The Prapañcasāra (attributed to Śaṅkara) frames mantra practice non-dualistically, while the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati follows Śaiva Siddhānta.
